claims.text: The nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The nanoparticles are initially crystallized as a solid solution.
Structural and chemical stability is primarily governed by entropy of mixing.
Entropy of mixing stabilizes the solid-solution phase over 473–1923 K.
Increasing temperature strengthens the entropic stabilization of the solid solution.
After thermal cycling between 473 K and 1923 K, the nanoparticles will retain structural stability relative to their room-temperature initial state.
After thermal cycling between 473 K and 1923 K, the nanoparticles will retain chemical stability relative to their room-temperature initial state.
Only minimal phase separation or degradation will occur during thermal cycling.
An inert atmosphere prevents oxidation or contamination during testing.
A controlled thermal environment provides uniform heating and cooling.
The proposed mechanism need not apply to systems containing fewer than five metals or substantially non-equiatomic ratios.
The specific metal combination and constituent thermodynamic properties may change the degree and temperature range of stability.
X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive spectroscopy can be used to compare the material before and after thermal cycling.
Observation of significant phase separation or structural degradation after thermal cycling would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and prediction categorically assert stability throughout 473–1923 K, while the uncertainty field says the exact temperature range of stability depends on the metal combination. This makes the stated universal range internally overconfident relative to its caveat.
